newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- January CPI to be focus this week.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- January CPI to be focus this week.

text.p: The January Consumer Price Index (CPI), due on Wednesday, is expected to be the focal point for the U.S. government securities market in the coming week, said market analysts.
Still, some wondered whether even the CPI would prove that eventful and they added that buyer interest might not persist if the 30-year Treasury bond yield reached 6.50 percent.
The market closed higher for the week after plowing through a $39.75 billion Treasury refinancing. The 30-year Treasury bond ended at 101-8/32, yielding 6.53 percent.
The market closed early of Friday before the Presidents Day three-day holiday weekend. U.S. financial markets will be closed on Monday to observe the holiday.
"I think you're going to lose buyer interest for sure at 6.50-ish (on the bond yield)," said William Sullivan, senior vice president and fixed-income research director at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Sullivan said for practical purposes, "the final (economic) number for the month is the CPI.
"Then the market is on hold," he said. "That doesn't mean it can't go up, down or sideways, but the (major movements) come to an end for February when we get the CPI."
Economists polled by Reuters believe the CPI rose 0.3 percent in January after a 0.3 percent December rise.
The core CPI, the price index without its more volatile food and energy items, is forecast to have risen 0.2 percent after a slight 0.1 percent December gain.
Even though the CPI might provide the most prominent headline of the week, the market might take a sanguine view of it, economists said.

"There's just no passing through of higher wages to final prices yet so I don't think we're really sitting on the edge of our seats waiting for the government to tell us that inflation is rising," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo - Mitsubishi.

"One bad CPI would not change the debate that much," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. "It would come out of the blue and would look strange. There's just not much threatening yet on the inflation side."
The market will also get U.S. international trade data for December on Wednesday.
The trade deficit is expected to widen to $9.9 billion, according to a Reuters poll, after a relatively narrow $8.4 billion gap was recorded in November.
"Trade could be interesting this time because we were so low recently," said Rupkey.
"If the deficit goes up, that will hack away at some of the 4.7 percent GDP growth that we saw in the fourth quarter and could put downward pressure on first quarter estimates," Rupkey said.
A batch of three economic releases due on Thursday should draw some market attention.

January housing starts, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, are expected to total 1.42 million on an annualized basis, up from a similarly adjusted December housing starts total of 1.329 million. The Philadelphia Fed survey, which read +11.3 in Janaury, is expected to read +10.0 in February, according to a Reuters poll.
Weekly jobless claims, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Thursday, are expected to total 323,000 for the week ended February 15 after totaling 309,000 a week earlier.
Glassman said jobless claims data are noteworthy.

"Last fall when the Fed said things were slowing down, jobless claims were the only data that said otherwise," he said. Glassman said claims rose after Thanksgiving, but that much of that was related to disruptive weather on the West Coast when agriculture workers are quick to be laid off and quick to file for unemployment insurance.
"Jobless claims near 330,000 would suggest that the economy still has a lot of momentum," said Glassman.
